pages.name: Two arrows
pages.text: The pull's angle is a direction. The turning arrow's angle is a time. A 3 kN pull on a ring points the way its rope runs. Beside it, an arrow turns once a cycle, and its height traces a [[sine wave]]. Frozen at one instant, it is the [[phasor]], the fixed arrow `r∠θ`. Frozen at 45°, it is 2.5 ms into the cycle.

pages.name: How much later
pages.task: A current is 90° behind the voltage. How much later does the current peak?
pages.why: A whole turn is 360° and takes 20 ms. 90° is a quarter of that. So the current peaks 20 × 90 ÷ 360 = 5 ms after the voltage. The angle measures a delay. Nothing in the cable points that way.

pages.name: Adding
pages.text: Two 3 kN pulls, square to each other, add nose to tail to 4.24 kN. Two 3 A currents a quarter turn apart add the same way, to 4.24 A. At every instant the sum's height is their two heights added. They turn together, so the sum turns with them.
pages.alt: On the left, two 3 kN pulls square to each other, nose to tail, make 4.24 kN. On the right, two 3 A currents a quarter turn apart, nose to tail, make 4.24 A, and all three arrows turn together. Their heights stack on the upright line: 2.6 and −1.5 make the sum's 1.1. Beside them, the three waves.

pages.name: Two currents
pages.task: 6 A flows in step with the voltage. Another 8 A is a quarter turn behind. What is the total current?
pages.why: Lay them nose to tail. The 8 A runs square to the 6 A. So the total is √(6² + 8²) = 10 A, not 14 A.

pages.name: Two speeds
pages.text: A 50 Hz arrow and a 150 Hz arrow start together. The faster one turns three times as fast, so the angle between them keeps changing. That is why waves of different frequencies cannot share one phasor diagram.
pages.alt: A 50 Hz arrow and a 150 Hz arrow turn from one point, 2.5 ms after starting together. The 50 Hz one has turned 45° and the 150 Hz one 135°, so the faster one is 90° ahead. Beside them, the waves they trace over 20 ms.

pages.name: After 5 ms
pages.task: Both arrows start together at 0°. How far apart are they 5 ms later?
pages.why: In 5 ms the 50 Hz arrow makes a quarter turn, 90°. The 150 Hz arrow turns three times as far, 270°. So they are 270° − 90° = 180° apart.
pages.alt: A 50 Hz arrow and a 150 Hz arrow from one point, both starting at 0°, with the waves they trace over 20 ms. The first 5 ms is marked. After 5 ms the 50 Hz arrow has turned 90° and the 150 Hz arrow 270°, so they point opposite ways, 180° apart.

pages.name: Dividing
pages.text: Written as a number, a phasor can be divided. A force arrow cannot be divided like this. Divide the sizes and take away the angles. So `230∠0° V` ÷ `10∠−30° A` gives an [[impedance]] of `23∠30° Ω`. From here the arrows are drawn at rms, the size a meter reads. The turning arrows were drawn at the peak, and drawings differ on which to use.

pages.name: Divide it
pages.task: Divide `230∠0° V` by `5∠−60° A`. What is the impedance?
pages.why: Divide the sizes: 230 ÷ 5 = 46 Ω. Take away the angles: 0° − (−60°) = 60°. So the impedance is `46∠60° Ω`. Multiplying does the opposite. It multiplies the sizes and adds the angles. So V times I as numbers is not true power. True power uses the angle between them, in VI cos φ.

pages.name: Three phases
pages.text: Three phase currents leave the star point 120° apart. Whatever the lines carry out must come back on the neutral. So the neutral carries their nose-to-tail sum. With pure 50 Hz sine waves, three equal 10 A currents close like the ring's pulls, so the neutral carries 0 A. Shorten one and the chain falls short, leaving a gap that is the [[neutral current]].

pages.name: One line light
pages.task: L1 and L2 carry 10 A each. L3 carries 4 A. What does the neutral carry?
pages.why: Across: 10 − 5 − 2 = 3 A. Up: 0 − 8.66 + 3.46 = −5.20 A. So the neutral carries √(3² + 5.20²) = 6 A, not 24 A. When two lines match, the neutral carries the difference, 10 − 4 = 6 A.

pages.name: Line to line
pages.task: Take `230∠−120° V` away from `230∠0° V`. What is the voltage between the two lines?
pages.why: Turn `230∠−120° V` round to get `230∠60° V`, then add. Across: 230 + 115 = 345 V. Up: 0 + 199.19 = 199.19 V. So the line voltage is √(345² + 199.19²) = 398 V, at 30°. That is √3 × 230 V, the 400 V between lines you know from three-phase boards.
